extracted.intended_audience: experimental physiologists, physiological chemists, and physical scientists conducting laboratory and field observations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for designing and conducting experiments and observations in physiological chemistry (and related atmospheric-electricity field work), emphasizing methods that reproduce in‑vivo conditions, use sensitive continuous recording, control environmental variables, and employ appropriate networks of observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous registration of physical phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing is so characteristic of modern methods in physical science as continuous registration of physical phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain continuous records (e.g., receiving a spot of light from the electrometer needle on a sensitized-paper-covered revolving cylinder driven by clock-work) so that 24-hour observations can be taken. Continuous recording captures transient or anomalous fluctuations that scattered, intermittent observations miss (example: recording movements of the human heart to study minute anomalies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of highly sensitive apparatus for atmospheric electricity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use methods sensitive enough to detect discharges of lightning even when the thunder-storm has not yet appeared above the horizon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example apparatus: an insulated tin can filled with flowing water connected to an electrometer quadrant; this method lets the can take on the electric charge of the air. Sensitive setups will show a throb of the electrometer-needle in advance of visible storms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Networked simultaneous observations at many stations
rubrics_metrics.description: Simultaneous observations are needed at a large number of stations to add to our knowledge of the electrical conditions of the air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a network requires fitting each station (~cost estimate given historically: ~$600) and experienced observers. Cooperation between colleges and the governmental Signal Service is recommended: begin with colleges, demonstrate value, then integrate into regular service. Demonstrate practical utility (e.g., storm-path prediction) to justify government establishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental reproduction of in vivo conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: We must endeavor to work under similar conditions and with the same means as the body itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform experiments at body temperature, avoid reagents whose presence would be injurious to the organism, and replicate physiological concentrations and environments. Avoid relying on high temperatures or strong reagents that would not be present in vivo (example: hippuric acid synthesis in lab requires heating to 160°C, whereas in the body it occurs in blood/kidney without such heating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate multi-step processes rather than single reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: We must take into consideration that we may not be able to attain our object by a single process, but by a whole series of altogether different processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments and interpretations that allow for sequences of reactions and intermediate steps rather than forcing a single-step mechanism; many physiological syntheses are multi-stage under mild conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require direct evidence before attributing action to a specific ferment
rubrics_metrics.description: The latter is not to be considered the effect of fermentation, until actual evidence of the presence of a specific ferment is furnished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume the action of a definite chemical ferment (enzyme) without isolation or demonstrable evidence. Historical failures to isolate an 'alcoholic ferment' in yeast justified considering vital cellular action as an alternative explanation. Positive attribution requires biochemical isolation or equivalent proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and account for internal cellular organization
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems much more simple and natural to suppose that each of the reactions takes place separately, which could be most readily effected by an internal organization of the cell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating protoplasm as homogeneous; design experiments and interpretations that allow for compartmentalization or internal structures within cells that localize different chemical processes (e.g., why some bacteria are harmless while others are destructive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual model of ferment action as at least two reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: The action of every ferment must be considered as consisting of at least two reactions: formation of a compound with the substrate and subsequent splitting with regeneration of the ferment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling or investigating enzyme action, include steps where the ferment forms a temporary compound with the substrate and is then regenerated. Though not experimentally proven for all real ferments at the time, this model explains catalytic action and should guide mechanistic experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and report environmental conditions due to ferment sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: These processes of fermentation ... are very sensitive to foreign influences: some will only take place in a completely neutral or slightly alkaline solution, others only in a slightly acid solution; they all progress most rapidly at a certain temperature, and even slight deviations ... sensibly retard the action of a ferment or completely arrest it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully control and document pH, temperature, concentration, and other conditions (example: pepsin acts exclusively in acid solutions, best in hydrochloric acid). Small deviations can change outcomes dramatically, so experimental reproducibility requires strict environmental control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and fix intermediate products experimentally
rubrics_metrics.description: Intermediate products are formed in the body which are generally directly decomposed and therefore withdrawn from observation, but which can be fixed by the introduction of foreign material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To study transient intermediates, use techniques that 'fix' them via introduced reagents or trapping methods so they can be identified. Introduced foreign compounds can protect intermediates from further decomposition, revealing otherwise hidden steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid destructive reagents and methods when emulating physiological synthesis
rubrics_metrics.description: We must employ no reagents whose presence would be injurious to the organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attempting to reproduce in vivo syntheses, prefer mild reagents and conditions compatible with living tissue or blood; do not rely on harsh reagents/conditions that cannot exist in the organism if the goal is to infer physiological mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve methods for purification and characterization of complex biomolecules
rubrics_metrics.description: The substances which are most important in the economy of the organism, the albuminoids ... are very little known ... We do not even know whether the albuminoids and similar compounds have ever been obtained in a pure state; their composition is therefore only approximately known; a good method for separating the different members of larger groups is a pious wish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize development of better separation, purification, and analytical methods to obtain pure albuminoids and other complex biological substances; accurate composition and intermediate-product identification depend on advances in these techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider electrical and thermal phenomena integral to physiological chemistry
rubrics_metrics.description: The organism also makes use of certain physical phenomena ... namely, the electric and the thermic. The former take part in the excitation of the nerves, perhaps also in some of the chemical processes; the latter are to be considered as the source of heat in warm-blooded animals as well as of the mechanical force developed by the different muscles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include measurements or considerations of electrical and thermal effects when studying physiological chemical processes (e.g., nerve excitation, heat production and mechanical work), since many reactions are accompanied by temperature changes and electrical phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate the role of dust/particulates in atmospheric condensation and electrical properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Dust, or impalpable saline particles, are necessary for the formation of clouds. Without dust ... we should always have cloudless skies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design experiments that compare evaporation/condensation in dust-deprived vs. dust-containing air (examples: passing air through cotton-wool to remove dust, burning wood or sulphur to introduce particles). Also test inductive capacity of dust-films and trace fluctuations in electric sparks through dust-free vs. dust-containing air to assess impact on atmospheric electricity.
